column4: The wretched are in the Fire with anguished breathing, opening a passage that compares the two kinds of continued afterlife existence.
The Fire's people abide there for the divinely appointed span, making explicit the punitive staying developed by the section.
The blessed abide in the Garden and receive a gift that is not cut off, the beneficial permanence opposite the Fire's barren continuance in 11:106-107.
The invoked beings are “dead, not living,” an exact lexical reversal that distinguishes lifeless nonentities from the section's conscious state that is neither completed death nor true life.
God is the Living, the Sustainer, whom neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes; perfect life without sleep sharply contrasts the inmate's denied, restorative sleep and empty nondeath.
The followers wish for a return to disown their leaders, but they will not emerge from the Fire, another concrete denial of an endpoint to punishment.
The wrongdoers are told to taste “the punishment of permanence,” directly naming the destructive lastingness distinguished from true lasting life.
The Fire is called the enemies of God's “home of permanence,” locating everlasting duration in the punitive counterpart to the Hereafter's true life.
The condemned remain under the curse with punishment neither lightened nor delayed, specifying continued existence without relief.
When wrongdoers see punishment, it is neither lightened nor postponed, closing both relief and delay as exits from the section's nonlife.
The person given his record behind his back calls for destruction, voicing the condemned person's wish that death finish what judgment has begun.
He enters a blazing fire after calling for destruction in 84:11, locating that impossible wish inside the section's punishment scene.
God creates death and life as the field of testing, placing both endpoints under purposeful creation before the afterlife condition in which neither provides release.
Human beings live on earth, die there, and are brought out from it, a complete ordinary sequence against which the Fire's blocked death and life stand out.
After the stages of earthly creation, human beings will die, marking death as a true transition rather than the endless attenuation described in the Fire.
After death people are raised on Resurrection Day, completing the sequence whose endpoints 87:13 deliberately denies within Hell.
God gives life, causes death, and gathers everyone for the Day of Resurrection, correcting the worldly-only account of dying and living in 45:24.
God gives life, causes death, and remains as inheritor, joining divine control of both endpoints to what remains when creatures pass.
God has apportioned death among people and cannot be outstripped, establishing death as a measured divine boundary rather than an escape available at will.
God can replace people with their likes and create them in a form they do not know, completing 56:60's claim that continued existence and transformation remain His act.
Every soul tastes death before being returned to God, a universal mortal boundary that makes Hell's refusal to complete death exceptional.
Every soul tastes death and then returns to God, repeating the ordinary passage from nearer life to the lasting destination.
At Uḥud some desired worldly gain and others desired the Hereafter, a concrete enactment of the preference diagnosed in 87:16.
Those who exchange worldly life for the Hereafter are told to fight, presenting the saving inverse of preferring the nearer life.
Worldly enjoyment is declared little and the Hereafter better for the God-conscious, a close verbal counterpart to 87:16-17.
Some desire the goods of this world while God desires the Hereafter for them, setting immediate acquisition against the divinely valued destination.
The ayah separates whoever wants worldly reward from whoever wants the reward of the Hereafter, casting the section's preference as an actionable intention.
One promised a good promise and meeting it is contrasted with one briefly furnished with worldly enjoyment and then brought to judgment.
Those desiring worldly life wish for Qārūn's visible fortune, dramatizing how the near good attracts preference.
People of knowledge answer that God's reward is better for faith and good action, correcting the worldly desire voiced in 28:79.
People know only the outward appearance of worldly life while remaining heedless of the Hereafter, explaining how nearness hides the lasting life.
Worldly luxury is only temporary enjoyment, while the Hereafter with the Lord belongs to the mindful, directly revaluing apparent benefit by permanence.
Worldly life is play and diversion, reducing the object of preference to passing occupation rather than true life.
The person who turns from remembrance wants only worldly life, joining rejection of reminder to the near-life preference that ends in loss.
Those who do good receive good here, but the home of the Hereafter is better, locating goodness fully in the destination the section calls better and more lasting.
The question asks why earlier generations lacked “people of remainder” who restrained corruption, joining the ب ق ي root to preserved moral good.
Abraham leaves the declaration of God's oneness as “a word remaining” among his descendants, a constructive kind of survival through transmission.
At resurrection the guilty whisper that they remained only ten days, exposing the nearer life's apparent length as brief from the lasting side.
The most perceptive say they remained only a day, intensifying the collapse of worldly duration begun in 20:103.
God asks how many years people remained on earth, forcing the condemned to measure the life they preferred against their present destination.
They answer that they remained a day or part of a day, recognizing the nearer life's brevity.
God confirms that they remained only a little, if they had known, making their former preference a failure of temporal judgment.
Earlier messengers ate food and were not immortal, setting bodily life and its needs within a mortal limit despite prophetic rank.
Believers who do good receive the Gardens of Paradise as hospitality, introducing beneficial afterlife continuance rather than mere survival.
They abide in Paradise and desire no transfer from it, the fulfilled permanence opposite the Fire's inhabitants who plead for an end or exit.
The servants of the Merciful abide in the lofty chambers, which are praised as a good settlement and residence; goodness and staying coincide there.
The command is to seek the home of the Hereafter with God's gift while not forgetting one's worldly share, defining a boundary between proper use and preference.
God gives life and causes death, and all return to Him; the repeated formula confirms that both transitions and their destination belong to one Lord.
God gives life and causes death alongside the alternation of night and day, embedding the two endpoints in an ordered cycle rather than random loss.
God gives life and causes death by decisive command, reinforcing that the Fire's denied death is governed rather than accidental.
The sole God gives life and causes death and is Lord of present and former generations, extending His agency across every mortal span.
God gives life and causes death, and to Him is the destination, joining the endpoints to the final return.
God is the one who causes death and gives life, a concise attribution of the two poles negated for the Fire's inmate.
The possessor of all dominion gives life and causes death, grounding both states in the power that also determines permanence.
The Prophet cannot make the dead hear the call, using death for lost responsiveness and sharpening the section's beneficial sense of life.
The same inability to make the dead hear recurs, marking receptive hearing as a form of life beyond biological duration.
The skeptic displays decayed bones and asks who can give them life, turning loss of bodily power into an explicit challenge about restoration.
The answer says the One who originated the bones will revive them, resolving 36:78's apparent extinction with divine life-giving power.
After distress, drowsiness descends as security upon part of the believers, showing sleep as a restorative good unavailable in the section's punishment.
God covers the believers with drowsiness as security, another specific instance of sleep conveying protection and benefit.
Sleep is made for rest, directly identifying the good contained in the deathlike interval that the Fire's inmate cannot enjoy.
Turning from God's reminder brings a constricted living, a life-form whose deprivation helps distinguish biological duration from beneficial life.
Water is driven to barren land and brings forth crops eaten by people and animals, an indirect but concrete meeting of water, restored productivity, and benefit.
When the Hour rises, the guilty swear they remained only an hour, showing worldly duration collapsing at resurrection.
Those given knowledge correct them: they remained until the Day of Resurrection, distinguishing the measured nearer stay from the lasting reality now reached.
The death people flee will meet them before their return to the Knower, denying escape from the normal transition even as the condemned later seek death as release.
Paradise contains rivers of water that never alters, giving the source section's life-giving Paradise water a Quranic counterpart in unspoiled permanence.
